source.title: Interpreting CLIP with Hierarchical Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Vladimir Zaigrajew; Hubert Baniecki; P. Biecek

record.tranche_reason: The paper tests Matryoshka SAE reconstruction and progressive recovery, but does not test whether features in a smaller dictionary correspond to sets of features in a larger dictionary, or whether those sets partition inputs.
record.gate_note: The progressive-recovery results are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version: they measure reconstruction as more SAE activations are used, not feature splitting or geometric relationships between features across dictionary sizes. General SAE fidelity, sparsity, concept-mapping, and application results do not test the claim. The paper mentions feature absorption as one possible explanation for decoder non-orthogonality, but reports no new absorption test.
record.test_reason: This paper proposes a Matryoshka SAE for CLIP that nests TopK over the number of active latents (k), not over dictionary size. It reports reconstruction, sparsity, alignment, orthogonality, concept-naming and progressive-recovery results. It never compares features across dictionary sizes, never measures parent/child firing (absorption), and never measures feature splitting. Absorption is mentioned only as one possible cause of decoder non-orthogonality. It neither tests nor relies on any version of the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that MSAE gives a better sparsity–fidelity Pareto frontier for CLIP (0.99 cosine similarity, under 0.1 FVU, about 80% sparsity), shows progressive recovery, and yields over 120 validated concepts usable for similarity search and bias analysis.
record.recipe_differences: The paper introduces Matryoshka SAE, training with multiple increasing TopK granularities and combined reconstruction losses. Its progressive-recovery evaluation does not match the cross-dictionary feature matching and input-partitioning measurements in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported progressive-recovery curves compare SAE architectures and activation thresholds; the text describes different behavior across architectures and metrics.

fits_no_version.finding: In progressive recovery (top-k activations by magnitude at inference), MSAE improves continuously, TopK plateaus near its training k, and ReLU improves but performs worse at high sparsity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAEs trained with nested multi-k TopK objectives support progressive reconstruction, whereas single-k TopK SAEs plateau beyond their training k.

record.problems: For the related progressive-recovery result, the supplied text gives qualitative figure descriptions rather than numeric values; the plotted values cannot be assigned precisely from the text. This evidence does not measure feature splitting or cross-dictionary correspondence.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-bearing cross-dictionary feature-splitting results are reported. Progressive-recovery extensions in Figures 16 and 17 are not extracted separately because they extend the same related measure across further expansion rates and modalities without testing any listed claim version.

untested.parts: All: no cross-dictionary-size feature matching, coverage or direction similarity.
All: no splitting measured in CLIP or in other SAE families.
All: no measurement of nested, geometrically close feature families. Hierarchy here refers to nested TopK sets over k.
All: absorption is only cited as a possible cause of non-orthogonality; no parent/child firing test.
All: no decomposition of larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE latents, and no count of novel latents.
All: this Matryoshka variant nests over k, not dictionary prefixes, and its effect on splitting is not measured.

record.verdict_notes: Appendix A gives a qualitative remark that a 'mammal' concept matches both 'cat' and 'dog' neurons. It is framed as a concept-naming limitation, not a measured hierarchy or splitting result. Table 3 counts valid concept neurons across expansion rates 8/16/32, but this is a concept-naming yield, not feature splitting. Section 4.5 mentions feature absorption (citing Chanin et al.) only as a speculative source of non-orthogonality.

versions.untested_parts: Whether larger dictionaries replace smaller-dictionary features with multiple more specific features that cover the same inputs and lie near the smaller feature's direction.
Whether size-based feature splitting holds in large models or open SAE releases.
Whether split features form nested, geometrically close families that mirror a hierarchy of concepts.
Whether a parent latent fails to fire when a child takes over, and whether changing SAE size or sparsity remedies this.
Whether larger-SAE latents decompose into combinations of smaller-SAE latents, and whether larger dictionaries add novel latents.
Whether splitting is caused by the SAE objective on correlated or hierarchical inputs, and whether Matryoshka SAEs change or reduce splitting.
